title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
hook: You can prune over 90% of a trained network and keep its accuracy. The catch: a tiny 'winning ticket' subnetwork was hiding inside the dense one from the start.
key_points: Pruning can remove over 90% of a network's parameters without sacrificing accuracy.
A dense random network contains small subnetworks — 'winning tickets' — that train as well alone.
Tickets match full accuracy in comparable iterations, trained from their original initialization.
An algorithm finds tickets under 10–20% of the original size on MNIST and CIFAR10.
content_html: Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin noticed that pruning can strip over 90% of a network's parameters with no loss in accuracy, and asked what that says about the original dense network. Their answer is the lottery ticket hypothesis: a dense, randomly-initialized network already contains small subnetworks — "winning tickets" — that can match the full network's accuracy when trained on their own.
extra_html:
How it works

The key condition is that a winning ticket is trained in isolation from its original initialization, not reinitialized from scratch. Under those conditions it reaches comparable accuracy in a comparable number of iterations to the full network. The authors give an algorithm to find such tickets and consistently turn up ones smaller than 10–20% of the original network on MNIST and CIFAR10.

Why it matters

The result reframes pruning: rather than shrinking a trained model after the fact, it suggests the small, trainable network was present at initialization all along. That has practical pull for efficiency and raises a deeper question about why initialization matters so much to whether a subnetwork can learn.

related.title: Deep Double Descent
related.hook: Bigger models should overfit, then get worse — right? Instead test error often dips, climbs, then dips again as model size grows, breaking the classic bias-variance story.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'winning ticket' in the lottery ticket hypothesis?
flashcards.back_html: A small subnetwork inside a dense, randomly-initialized network that can match the full network's accuracy when trained on its own.

flashcards.prompt: What condition is essential for a winning ticket to reach full accuracy?

choices.text: Training it from its original initialization, not reinitialized from scratch
Reinitializing it with fresh random weights before training
Pruning it only after it is fully trained in isolation

flashcards.explanation_html: The ticket must keep its original initialization; under that condition it matches full accuracy in a comparable number of iterations.
